# Software Implementation {.unnumbered}
 
Now that our hardware is wired for deep sleep, we need to restructure the firmware.

When the RTC alarm wakes the ESP32 up, it doesn't resume where it left off: it restarts from the beginning of `setup()`.

Therefore, in this deep-sleep design, **we do not use the `loop()` function at all**. All the logic (reading sensors, saving to SD, setting the next alarm, and going back to sleep) runs sequentially inside `setup()`.

## The Code

> **Further Reading:** The alarm logic used in this phase is adapted from the official [Adafruit RTClib DS3231_alarm example](https://github.com/adafruit/RTClib/blob/master/examples/DS3231_alarm/DS3231_alarm.ino). The [EOLab Deep Sleep Wiki](https://wiki.eolab.de/doku.php?id=amc2020:group_n:deepsleep) covers the same DS3231 + ESP32 setup in more depth.
>
> *(Note on the pull-up resistor: EOLab uses a 100kΩ pull-up on `SQW` to minimize the current drawn while the alarm is active. We use 10kΩ, which draws a bit more during the few milliseconds the alarm is active, but gives a stiffer, less noise-sensitive signal. Both work.)*

> **Ready-to-use project:** The complete code for this power management phase is available in the repository here: [`05_power_management_rtc`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/main/firmware/PoC/Phase-02/05_power_management_rtc)

```cpp
/*
 * Project: Personal Autonomous Weather Station
 * Phase 02: Power Management
 * File: 05_power_management_rtc.ino
 * 
 * Description:
 * This sketch implements a fully autonomous deep sleep architecture.
 * The ESP32 relies on a DS3231 RTC to wake it up via an external
 * interrupt (EXT0).
 * Upon waking, it reads the BME280 sensor, powers ON the SD card, saves the 
 * data with an accurate timestamp, schedules the next RTC alarm, and
 * immediately returns to deep sleep to conserve battery.
 *
 * Wiring:
 * - BME280:  3.3V -> VIN, GND -> GND, Pin 21 -> SDA, Pin 22 -> SCL
 * - DS3231:  3.3V -> VCC, GND -> GND, Pin 21 -> SDA, Pin 22 -> SCL, 
 *            Pin 36 -> SQW (Requires a 10k pull-up resistor to 3.3V)
 * - SD Card: 5V   -> VCC, GND -> GND, Pin 19 -> MISO, Pin 23 -> MOSI, 
 *            Pin 18 -> SCLK, Pin 5 -> CS, 
 *            Pin 13 -> OFF (Requires a 10k pull-down resistor to GND)
 */

#include <Arduino.h>
#include <Adafruit_Sensor.h>
#include <Adafruit_BME280.h>
#include <SPI.h>
#include <SD.h>
#include <FS.h>
#include <RTClib.h>

#define SD_CS_PIN 5
#define SD_OFF_PIN 13
#define RTC_WAKEUP_PIN 36

// Offset between your computer's local time and UTC, in seconds.
// Used only to convert the compile time to UTC when setting the RTC.
// Example: Paris is UTC+1 in winter (3600) and UTC+2 in summer (7200).
#define COMPILE_TIME_UTC_OFFSET 7200

Adafruit_BME280 bme;
RTC_DS3231 rtc;

// How often should the station wake up to take a reading? 
// (In seconds for testing)
const int WAKEUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 30;

void appendFile(fs::FS &fs, const char * path, const char * message) {
  File file = fs.open(path, FILE_APPEND);
  if (file) {
    file.print(message);
    file.close();
  }
}

void print_wakeup_reason(){
  esp_sleep_wakeup_cause_t wakeup_reason = esp_sleep_get_wakeup_cause();
  switch(wakeup_reason) {
    case ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_EXT0: 
      Serial.println("Wakeup by external signal using RTC_IO (RTC Alarm)"); 
      break;
    case ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_EXT1: 
      Serial.println("Wakeup by external signal using RTC_CNTL"); 
      break;
    case ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_TIMER: 
      Serial.println("Wakeup caused by timer"); 
      break;
    case ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_TOUCHPAD: 
      Serial.println("Wakeup caused by touchpad"); 
      break;
    case ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_ULP: 
      Serial.println("Wakeup caused by ULP program"); 
      break;
    default: 
      Serial.printf("Wakeup was not caused by deep sleep: %d\n", wakeup_reason);
      break;
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Serial.println("\n--- Waking up from Deep Sleep ---");
  
  print_wakeup_reason();

  // 1. Initialize RTC
  if (!rtc.begin()) {
    Serial.println("Couldn't find RTC");
    Serial.flush();
    esp_deep_sleep_start(); // Sleep forever if RTC fails
  }

  // If the RTC lost power (e.g., battery died or first time use),
  // set the time to the compile time. We don't do this unconditionally
  // to avoid resetting the time on every deep sleep wake-up.
  if (rtc.lostPower()) {
    Serial.println("RTC lost power, setting the time to compile time!");
    // __DATE__ and __TIME__ are in local time: convert them to UTC.
    DateTime compileTime(F(__DATE__), F(__TIME__));
    rtc.adjust(compileTime - TimeSpan(COMPILE_TIME_UTC_OFFSET));
  }

  // Read the time immediately after waking up for maximum accuracy!
  DateTime now = rtc.now();

  // Power optimizations & alarm resets
  rtc.disable32K(); // Disable the 32kHz output to save power
  // Stop oscillating signals at SQW Pin (required for alarms)
  rtc.writeSqwPinMode(DS3231_OFF); 
  rtc.disableAlarm(2); // Disable Alarm 2 so it doesn't accidentally trigger
  
  // Clear any existing alarm flags so the SQW pin goes back HIGH
  rtc.clearAlarm(1);
  rtc.clearAlarm(2);

  // 2. Initialize BME280 and read data
  if (bme.begin(0x76)) {
    // Forced mode: the sensor takes one measurement on demand, then goes
    // back to sleep (the library default, normal mode, measures non-stop).
    bme.setSampling(Adafruit_BME280::MODE_FORCED,
                    Adafruit_BME280::SAMPLING_X1,  // temperature
                    Adafruit_BME280::SAMPLING_X1,  // pressure
                    Adafruit_BME280::SAMPLING_X1,  // humidity
                    Adafruit_BME280::FILTER_OFF);
    bme.takeForcedMeasurement();
  } else {
    Serial.println("Could not find a valid BME280 sensor!");
  }
  float temperature = bme.readTemperature();
  float humidity = bme.readHumidity();
  float pressure = bme.readPressure() / 100.0F;

  // Format the data string using the built-in toString method
  char timestamp[] = "YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss";
  now.toString(timestamp);

  char dataString[100];
  sprintf(dataString, "%s;%.2f;%.2f;%.2f\n", 
          timestamp, temperature, humidity, pressure);
          
  Serial.print("Data: ");
  Serial.print(dataString);

  // 3. Power ON the SD Card and save data
  pinMode(SD_OFF_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(SD_OFF_PIN, HIGH);
  delay(100); // Wait for the SD card to power up and stabilize

  if (SD.begin(SD_CS_PIN)) {
    // Create header if file doesn't exist
    if (!SD.exists("/weather_data.csv")) {
      File file = SD.open("/weather_data.csv", FILE_WRITE);
      if (file) {
        file.println("timestamp;temperature;humidity;pressure");
        file.close();
      }
    }
    appendFile(SD, "/weather_data.csv", dataString);
    Serial.println("Data saved to SD card.");
  } else {
    Serial.println("Failed to mount SD card.");
  }

  // Power OFF the SD card module
  SD.end();
  digitalWrite(SD_OFF_PIN, LOW);

  // 4. Set the next wake-up alarm
  // To wake up on a fixed grid (e.g., exactly at :00 and :30 seconds),
  // we calculate the next interval boundary using Unix time (seconds
  // since 1970).
  // Read the time again: the work above took some time, and an alarm set
  // in the past would only fire the next day (it matches H:M:S).
  uint32_t currentUnix = rtc.now().unixtime();
  uint32_t remainder = currentUnix % WAKEUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS;
  uint32_t nextAlarmUnix = currentUnix - remainder + WAKEUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS;
  DateTime future(nextAlarmUnix);
  
  // Set Alarm 1 to trigger when the time matches.
  // Note: DS3231_A1_Hour is confusingly named! It actually means 
  // "Match Hours, Minutes, and Seconds". This ensures the alarm fires 
  // exactly once at the future time we just calculated.
  if (!rtc.setAlarm1(future, DS3231_A1_Hour)) {
      Serial.println("Error, alarm wasn't set!");
  } else {
      Serial.printf("Next reading scheduled for: %02d:%02d:%02d\n", 
                    future.hour(), future.minute(), future.second());
  }

  // 5. Configure ESP32 Deep Sleep Wake-up Source
  // We use EXT0 to wake up when the RTC pulls pin 36 LOW
  esp_sleep_enable_ext0_wakeup((gpio_num_t)RTC_WAKEUP_PIN, 0);

  // 6. Go to Sleep
  Serial.println("Entering Deep Sleep...");
  Serial.flush();
  esp_deep_sleep_start();
}

void loop() {
  // We never reach the loop() because esp_deep_sleep_start() halts execution!
}
```

## How It Works

1.  **Print Wake-up Reason:** The helper function `print_wakeup_reason()` shows what triggered the boot: our RTC alarm (`EXT0`) or a standard power-on.
2.  **Conditional Time Setting (`lostPower`):** We do *not* set the time unconditionally with `rtc.adjust()`: it would reset the clock to the compile time at every wake-up. The time is only set if the RTC reports a power loss (first use, or coin cell removed or depleted). As in Phase 01, the compile time is converted to UTC.
3.  **RTC Configuration:** We disable the 32 kHz output (`rtc.disable32K()`), which also saves a little power, switch the SQW pin to interrupt mode (`rtc.writeSqwPinMode(DS3231_OFF)`), and disable the unused Alarm 2 (`rtc.disableAlarm(2)`).
4.  **Clear Alarms:** When an alarm triggers, the DS3231 sets an alarm flag and pulls SQW LOW. This flag is *latched*: SQW stays LOW until the flag is cleared over I2C. `rtc.clearAlarm(1)` and `rtc.clearAlarm(2)` release the SQW line, so that it goes back HIGH and can signal the next alarm.
5.  **BME280 in Forced Mode:** By default, the Adafruit library configures the BME280 in *normal mode*: the sensor measures continuously, and it keeps doing so while the ESP32 sleeps, since it is still powered. This wastes several hundred µA (see the [power budget](02-hardware-modifications.qmd#power-budget-estimates)) and slightly heats the sensor, which biases the temperature. We switch it to **forced mode** with `setSampling()`: `takeForcedMeasurement()` triggers a single measurement, after which the sensor automatically returns to sleep. The settings we use (1x oversampling, no filter) are the ones recommended by Bosch for weather monitoring.
6.  **Sequential Execution:** We read the sensor, turn on the SD card using `SD_OFF_PIN`, save the data with `now.toString()` for the timestamp, unmount the card with `SD.end()`, and turn it back off.
7.  **Set the Next Alarm (Grid Snapping):** We compute the next alarm on a fixed grid: `next = now - (now % interval) + interval`. With a 30-second interval, the station wakes up at `16:00:00`, `16:00:30`, `16:01:00`, and so on. If a wake-up happens off-grid (after a reset, or a manual wake-up in Phase 3), the next one automatically realigns on the grid.
    *   We read the time **again** right before computing the alarm, instead of reusing the timestamp read at wake-up. If the work done during the wake-up (SD card, and later Wi-Fi) takes longer than the interval, an alarm computed from the wake-up time would already be in the past. Because the alarm matches hours, minutes and seconds (see below), it would then only fire **the next day**.
    *   *The `DS3231_A1_Second` Gotcha:* The official [Adafruit RTClib DS3231_alarm example](https://github.com/adafruit/RTClib/blob/master/examples/DS3231_alarm/DS3231_alarm.ino) uses the `DS3231_A1_Second` flag, which means **"match only the seconds"**. It works for their 10-second demo, but with a 15-minute interval the alarm would fire every minute, whenever the seconds match.
    *   We use `DS3231_A1_Hour` instead. The name is misleading, but it means **"match hours, minutes and seconds"**: the alarm fires once, at the exact time we computed, for any interval shorter than a day.
8.  **Go to Sleep:** We tell the ESP32 to wake up when `RTC_WAKEUP_PIN` (Pin 36) goes LOW, and call `esp_deep_sleep_start()`. If the alarm time is reached between `setAlarm1()` and the start of deep sleep, nothing is lost: the latched SQW line is already LOW, and the ESP32 wakes up immediately.

## Expected Output

When you run the code, you should see the ESP32 align on the 30-second grid, take a reading, and go back to sleep:

```text
--- Waking up from Deep Sleep ---
Wakeup by external signal using RTC_IO (RTC Alarm)
Data: 2026-07-22T15:47:00;29.33;33.06;997.36
Data saved to SD card.
Next reading scheduled for: 15:47:30
Entering Deep Sleep...

--- Waking up from Deep Sleep ---
Wakeup by external signal using RTC_IO (RTC Alarm)
Data: 2026-07-22T15:47:30;29.42;32.79;997.32
Data saved to SD card.
Next reading scheduled for: 15:48:00
Entering Deep Sleep...
```

*(Note: You will also see some ESP32 bootloader logs like `rst:0x5 (DEEPSLEEP_RESET)` printed between cycles. This is normal.)*

And if you pull the SD card and check `weather_data.csv`, you will see aligned data points:

```csv
timestamp;temperature;humidity;pressure
2026-07-22T15:47:00;29.33;33.06;997.36
2026-07-22T15:47:30;29.42;32.79;997.32
```

## Next Steps

The station now spends most of its time in deep sleep, keeps the BME280 asleep between measurements, and powers the SD card only when writing. According to our [estimates](02-hardware-modifications.qmd#power-budget-estimates), the remaining consumption in deep sleep is dominated by the modules around the ESP32, not by the ESP32 itself.

Next, we transmit this data to a server over Wi-Fi.
